comment_text: Thanks to everyone who shared their thoughts here, whether positive or critical. I know "AI art" is a sensitive and divisive topic, and I completely respect the concerns many of you have raised.  To be clear: I don’t see AI as a replacement for creativity or design. I still start every project with sketches, ideas, and decisions that come from me. Tools like Adobe Firefly are just one part of my process, helping me iterate faster and explore different directions. As stated in the video I don’t ever use generated images as final output, I use them for inspiration, reference, or pieces I can adapt.  I’ve been working as a designer for over 20 years, and my goal with this channel has always been to share how new tools – whether Photoshop, Illustrator, or now AI – can fit into a designer’s workflow without replacing design fundamentals. You don’t have to agree with my take, but I hope we can keep this space open for discussion and learning.  I truly value all of you in this community, even if we see things differently. Thanks for watching and for holding me accountable as I continue to explore where design and technology meet.

video_title: From Sketch to AI Art: My Workflow With Adobe Firefly's Image Generator
comment_text: It depends if you consider yourself artist and/or if you consider yourself as a designer.  If you regard yourself as an artist, I still strongly think generative AI does not produce art. Using a base sketch helps, but the rendering afterwards is not art.  As a designer, where it’s more umbrella, and the priority is the result, not the journey, you still have an issue where the generated image will have errors in it. If you had made the whole thing by hand, those mistakes would simply be your human fingerprint. If it’s machine-generated mistakes, it now becomes “insufficient quality control if you don’t fix them post-generation.”  Interestingly, the user needs to pay to generate the image. It’s money going to Adobe and not another artist whose style options you’d think would work well, and would use that money as income.  One risk with using generated images as moodboard/references/inspiration is that it has been shown that generative AI compounds biases. As you say, you need to ensure you’re in control of the creative process. Which I would ask, wouldn’t you have to be less alert if you didn’t use generative AI? The only motivation I can see for using it in workflow is: curiosity or a tight deadline. Creative deadlines are often pressured by our Capitalist society, who care about efficiency and economic value only.  In a vacuum, the video is quite interesting, and the tool looks fun to experiment with. But we’re not in a vacuum. And there’s still a lot of work that needs to be done in legal systems to ensure no one is getting exploited by this Pandora’s Box.

comment_text: I agree with your approach overall, but I think there’s an important twist. Even when you use AI to help you find better questions, you still have to be the one steering that process. You can’t just say ‘give me better questions’ and expect something meaningful. That’s cutting yourself out of the creative process.  A better approach is to start with your own questions and ask AI to critique them. Where are they vague? What assumptions are baked in? What’s missing? That way you’re guiding the refinement instead of outsourcing it.  The same thing applies creatively. If I ask AI to write lyrics, I’ll get something generic. But if I write something myself and ask what’s not working, the feedback can be very useful. It’s not very good at writing lyrics, but AI is great at pointing out obvious weaknesses that you might miss.  And this is where people go wrong: don’t say ‘find better words’ or ‘fix the meter.’ That’s a bad habit. You’re handing over the creative decisions. Instead, ask ‘what’s wrong with this?’ Then you do the work of fixing it.  AI is at its best when it sharpens your thinking, not when it replaces it. Even the questions about your questions need to be directed by you, or you’re just drifting.

comment_text: How would you feel if I wrote a poem about what it's like to live in Alaska, even though I've never visited that place? odes.py") -replace "from transformers import CLIPImageProcessor, BartTokenizerFast", "from transformers import CLIPImageProcessor, BartTokenizer as BartTokenizerFast" | Set-Content "E:\YOUR_COMFYUI\custom_nodes\comfyui-florence2

comment_text: Ive been seeing what i personally think are very dumb arguments because people are very misinformed. AI 'art' is considered art because the result is prompted by a creative process by a human being. BUT it is extremely unethical because so many generators use copyrighted creative work (animations, illustrations, books etc) published online as data for these results. To make it more ethical is to have a system that limits this issue. E.g have a system that ensures that copyrighted creative works are not made available for these genrators to use. The problem is that the world wide web is such an open domain it i would be very difficult to regulate this, tho i am curious how different countries will approach this.  AI art does NOT make art more accessible, it is simply another method of making something look good just like other art media, because it gets direct information from data things that looks good/ cool/ beautiful/ inspiring etc (baisically what the human brain does but the brain is way more complex in how it hds information. Emotions/ info and memory processing/trauma etc affect this) and showing it to people, whatever thing that moves people from seeing things captured or developed by a human being.  Accessiblility in art actually means having art be available to people from different walks if life, including disability, socio-economic status etc etc, like designing an  ergonomic paint brushes for people with severe hand injury for example according to the individual artist's needs and goals in what art they make in what medium, and that includes the use of AI art (again considered very largely unethical), or a company making a range of budget versions of common art supplies like paint or alcahole markers etc or affordable digital art software like Krita and Blender.  You still need knowledge of art fundamentals in order to make good AI 'art', so no, it has very little to do with accessibility, knowing th fact that there are also people who want to physically make art, like painting, or physically making an art piece on a digital canvas. The way you could say AI art is accessable is that the AI art websites and software are user friendly because of the Ul (user interface) design, which in itself if an art form in a partial sense 😂 so now the user doesn't need to write the code to scrape from the internet or particular database and just type in a bunch of keywords into a promt box. Saying AI art is accessible is just an excuse for being too lazy to learn to make art in the professional context specifically, because those are the people affected. I don't care if you play with the art by yourself on an app, as long as the people using those apps know that if unregulated, you are using that work unethically if you distribute it for money. The acessibility argument undermines the weight of the issue with copyright
